A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARECHO and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-metric speech prediction experiments under Base and Scale training configurations, together with tokenization, decoding, dependency, and efficiency analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds quantization reconstruction, teacher-forced decoding, MOS-specific, and metric-subset comparisons.

M1.justification: The architecture, autoregressive objective, randomized classifier chain, and two-step decoding remain unchanged. v1's Linear tokenization already uses evenly spaced percentiles; v2 clarifies this same default. Teacher-forced decoding is an experimental control, not a replacement for the proposed inference method.

E1.justification: The datasets, speech domains, and 87 prediction targets remain unchanged. The added MOS analyses concern metrics already included in Appendix F. Appendix J explicitly reuses the Base dataset without additional data; its subset experiments change supervision configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The main UniVERSA and UniVERSA-T comparator set is retained. Diagnostic comparisons expand to include uniform-over-value quantization against percentile binning (Table 3), teacher-forced ARECHO (Table 13), and single-metric or subset-trained ARECHO controls (Tables 15–19). No new competing model family is introduced.

E3.justification: v2 adds several evaluation designs: held-out quantize–dequantize reconstruction with 500/1000 bins, ground-truth-conditioned decoding, single-metric training, and subset-versus-fullset supervision with training data held fixed. Appendix H also adds BMAE. The existing main experiments retain their stated splits, model sizes, and training budgets.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token-size, beam-size, dependency-order, and efficiency studies, v2 tests quantization fidelity, error propagation under oracle conditioning, metric-dependent benefits of joint prediction, and possible negative transfer from unrelated targets. These additions substantially broaden the questions investigated in Appendices B, I, and J.

E5.justification: Both versions state that significance is evaluated through permutation testing, without adding procedural details, repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars. v2's recommendation to report uncertainty in deployment does not constitute new statistical reporting.

E6.justification: Rank-correlation values change throughout retained tables. For Base-development ARECHO, SRCC/KTAU change from 0.43/0.36 to 0.86/0.72 while MSE remains 25.73 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 10). v2 also adds BMAE and the reconstruction, teacher-forcing, MOS, and subset results, plus a greater-than-100-fold estimator-speed claim in Section 5. The PDFs do not explain the correlation revisions as model improvements.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, autoregressive factorization, and decoding algorithm are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation. Appendix B's explicit percentile-spacing expression restates v1's Linear rule; the additional binning and reconstruction descriptions clarify implementation.

C1.justification: The abstract adds an explicit claim that confidence-oriented decoding reduces error propagation. It also emphasizes reference-free subset querying, which was already described in v1. The three principal method contributions, application scope, and conclusion remain essentially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of quantization fidelity versus prediction difficulty, teacher forcing as a reference-dependent upper bound, differing benefits of inter-metric conditioning, and randomized ordering as protection against negative transfer. It also identifies ordinal-aware objectives as future work. Some interpretations overreach: Table 14's consistency claim conflicts with its URGENT-MOS results.

D1.justification: v2 adds an open-source code announcement and repository pointer, specifies decoding numerical tokens to bin centroids, and documents fitting reconstruction-test percentiles on Base data. It also describes controls for the new subset experiments. Existing architecture, optimizer, hardware, and training-budget disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Baccianella et al. (2009), Cao et al. (2020), and Gutiérrez et al. (2015), connecting BMAE and future ordinal-aware learning to prior research. The related-work section and positioning against existing speech evaluation frameworks otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Appendix B is locally rewritten, flexible inference and Section 5 receive expanded explanations, and new analysis and logo subsections are inserted. Appendix lettering changes accordingly. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained, rather than extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with Table 3 and Tables 13–19, adds a BMAE column to the complete results table, and introduces the logo in Figure 5. It also corrects the token-size table's Beam Size header to Token Bins. Existing dependency plots and the training-time chart are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The quantization clarification, added diagnostic experiments, and code pointer improve documentation and empirical coverage. However, unexplained revisions to retained correlations and inconsistencies in new evidence prevent a reliable net judgment. Table 13 reports development ARECHO MSE as 40.95 versus 25.73 in Table 1, while Table 14 claims consistent improvements despite URGENT-MOS favoring UniVERSA-T (MSE 0.20 versus 0.26). These issues weaken confidence in the added validation, leaving its overall benefit uncertain.
